title: Curse Of Knowledge
description: Once you know something, you cannot easily imagine what it’s like not to know it. This makes you a terrible communicator with novices and leads to frustration in teaching, selling, and relationships.
shortDescription: Once you know something, you cannot easily imagine what it’s like not to know it. This makes you a terrible communicator with novices and leads to frustration in teaching, selling, and relationships.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: Once you know something, you cannot easily imagine what it’s like not to know it. This makes you a terrible communicator with novices and leads to frustration in teaching, selling, and relationships.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: A software engineer explains a product to customers using jargon and is baffled that they “don’t get it.”
A parent helps a child with homework and can’t understand why “it’s so hard; it’s obvious!”
A negotiator assumes the other party sees the deal’s logic as clearly as they do, and is shocked when they resist.

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: Skipping foundational steps because “everyone knows that.”
Using technical terms without realizing they are technical.

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: You’re frustrated that someone doesn’t follow your explanation.
You’ve forgotten the last time you were confused about this topic.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: Knowledge integrates into our mental model so thoroughly that the prior state of ignorance is overwritten. We can’t retrieve it, so we anchor on our own perspective.

sections.title: Protection Strategy
content: When explaining, ask: “What do they currently know, and what do they need to know first?”
Use the “explain it like I’m five” test.
Have a non‑expert review your communication and flag anything unclear.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
content: Assuming the curse of knowledge is a sign of intelligence; it’s a sign of poor perspective‑taking.
Blaming the listener for not understanding rather than adjusting your message.

sections.title: Real Scenario
sections.content: A doctor explains a diagnosis using medical terminology. The patient nods, doesn’t understand a word, and fails to follow the treatment plan. The doctor is confused by the non‑compliance, attributing it to “carelessness” rather than her own opaque communication.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: The clearer something is to you, the harder it may be to explain. What’s obvious to you is invisible to them until you build the bridge.
